newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao wins bail after cheating charge.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao wins bail after cheating charge.

text.p: A Delhi judge granted indefinite bail to former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao on Wednesday, the same day he was formally charged with criminal conspiracy in a 1983 cheating case.
Rao, the first former or serving prime minister to face criminal charges, had pleaded not guilty to the cheating charge. He has also been charged in two other cases.

"It is ordered that the applicant-accused be released on furnishing bail bond in the sum of 100,000 rupees ($2,801) with one surety in the like amount, failing which the accused shall be sent to judicial custody," Judge Ajit Bharihoke's order said.
Rao's lawyers said a Delhi-based exporter would guarantee the former prime minister's court appearance.
After the bail hearing, Rao's lawyers were jubilant. "In one word, he (Rao) is very happy. Justice has been done," lawyer R.K. Anand told reporters.
The order said bail would last until the trial ended. The next trial hearings were set for November 26 and 27, they said.
Earlier, Bharihoke, at a separate session, had charged Rao, 75, for his alleged involvement in the cheating case.
It was the third formal set of charges against Rao, whose scandal-ridden Congress party suffered its worst general election defeat in May..
At the earlier hearing, Rao did not go to the witness box. The charge papers were brought to him by a court official who asked: "Do you plead guilty or not?"
Rao replied: "No, I claim to be tried."
Bharihoke said his court was also charging a Hindu guru, Chandraswami, and his assistant K.N. Agarwal, in the case. Both pleaded not guilty. Neither was granted bail.

The cheating case involves expatriate Indian businessman Lakhubhai Pathak, who claimed he paid $100,000 to Chandraswami in an unsuccessful attempt to win a government newsprint contract after Rao, then foreign minister, assured him at a meeting in a New York hotel that he would get the contract.
Rao has said he is innocent in the case and has denied he was in New York at the time of the alleged meeting. If convicted, he faces a possible seven-year prison sentence.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) opposed Rao's bail saying that releasing Rao could lead to evidence-tampering.
Rao resigned as president of the Congress party in September.
Other cases in which Rao has been charged by the CBI involve alleged forgery and vote-buying.

In the forgery case, Rao has been accused of colluding with Chandraswami in 1989 in an alleged attempt to defame rebel Congress leader V.P. Singh, who later defected and became the prime minister of India.

In the forgery case, on which Rao has not commented publicly, the Delhi High Court was scheduled to hear arguments seeking his bail on Thursday after a Delhi magistrate rejected a regular bail application on Tuesday.
Rao's lawyers said his bail chances in the forgery case have improved. "Once he is granted bail in one case, it should ordinarily be granted in the other," lawyer I.U. Khan said.

In the vote-buying case, Rao and his party colleagues are accused of playing a role in buying votes of deputies from a regional party in 1993 during a confidence motion in parliament which Rao's minority government won by a thin margin.
Rao has denied any wrongdoing in the case.
